essentialQuestion.source: How can you check a photo, video or voice before you trust it?
essentialQuestion.back: How can you check a photo, video or voice before trusting it?

learningGoal.source: Explain how AI can make realistic pictures, videos and voices, tell labelled creative work from a fake, and check the source before you trust or share one.
learningGoal.back: Explain how AI can make realistic pictures, videos and voices, tell creative work that has a label apart from fake content, and check the source before trusting or sharing it.
learningGoal.note: "Label" (an AI label on a post) is "keterangan" (caption, note) throughout, as the lesson already used for the goat video's caption; "label" is Lesson 3's word for training labels.

read.sections.0.heading.source: AI can make pictures, videos and voices
read.sections.0.heading.back: AI can make pictures, videos and voices

read.sections.0.text.source: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from enormous numbers of real examples, so what they make can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly and creatively. Artists make pictures, film makers add effects and teachers make lessons, and they say that AI helped. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”, so that is not a trick. A fake is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is a fake that copies a real person's face or voice, often to trick people for money or attention. Labels can get lost, too. If someone shares the goat video without its label, as if it were real, it can mislead people.
read.sections.0.text.back: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from real examples in very large numbers, so the results can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly and creatively. Artists make pictures, film makers add effects, and teachers make lessons, and they say that AI helped. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a video of a talking goat with the caption “Made with AI, just for fun”, so that is not a trick. Fake content is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is fake content that copies the face or voice of a real person, often to trick people for money or attention. Captions can also get lost. If someone shares the goat video without its caption, as if it were real, the video can mislead people.

Artists, film makers and teachers say when AI helped. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat. Its label says AI made it, just for fun. That is not a trick. A fake is different. It shows something that never happened, as if it were real. A deepfake copies a real person's face or voice to trick people. Labels can get lost too. Shared without its label, the goat video could fool people.

Fake content is different. Fake content shows something that never happened, as if it were real. A deepfake copies a real person's face or voice to trick people. Captions can get lost too. read.sections.1.heading.source: Strange details are clues, not proof
read.sections.1.heading.back: Strange details are clues, not proof

read.sections.1.text.source: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign or a background that melts into a wall. In a video, the mouth may not move with the words. These details can be clues, but they are not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake can look perfect. Real photographs can also look strange, for example when they are blurry or taken in poor light. In a 2025 study by researchers in the United States, more than 50,000 people judged real photos and AI pictures online. They wrongly called about one in four real photos AI-made, and they also missed about one in four AI pictures. The fruit seller's photo has very smooth skin, but the photo club says who took it, with a phone.
read.sections.1.text.back: AI-made pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign, or a background that merges into a wall. In a video, the mouth movement may not match the words. These details can be clues, but not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake picture can look perfect. Real photos can also look strange, for example when they are blurry or taken in a poorly lit place. In a 2025 study by researchers in the United States, more than 50,000 people judged real photos and AI-made pictures online. They wrongly called about one in four real photos AI-made, and they also took about one in four AI-made pictures for real photos. The fruit seller's photo shows very smooth skin, but the photo club says who took it, with a phone.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Missed about one in four AI pictures" is spelled out as "took them for real photos" (mengira ... sebagai foto asli), which is what the study measured.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real photos can look strange too, when they are dark or not sharp. In a 2025 study, more than 50,000 people looked at pictures online. Some were real, and some were AI. People called about one in four real photos AI-made. They also missed about one in four AI pictures. The fruit seller has very smooth skin. But the photo club says a phone took it.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: AI-made pictures sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real photos can look strange too, when they are dark or not sharp. In a 2025 study, more than 50,000 people looked at pictures online. Some were real, and some were AI-made. People called about one in four real photos AI-made. They also thought about one in four AI pictures were real. The fruit seller's skin is very smooth. But the photo club says the photo was taken with a phone.

read.sections.2.text.source: So the most useful check is the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from, and does the maker say how it was made? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? Make sure they did not all copy one post, because ten copies are still one source. Fact-checking groups do this work for pictures that spread widely. In Greenhill, the farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin, and a page with no name posted the photo. So that photo is probably fake. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you still can't tell, say so, and don't share it yet.
read.sections.2.text.back: So the most useful check is checking the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from, and does its maker say how the content was made? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? Make sure they did not all copy one post, because ten copies are still just one source. Fact-checking groups do this work for pictures that spread widely. In Greenhill, the farm's own official page says it did not grow a giant pumpkin, and the one that posted the photo is a page with no name. So the photo is probably fake. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you still can't be sure, say so, and don't share it yet.

watch.summary.source: This video comes from a series made with a team of teenage fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. AI pictures can have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check if the lips move with the words. For AI voices, listen to the tone and to the sounds in the background. The video also shows tools that can help, like a search that finds where else a picture appears online. But these tools are not always right. A person still needs to think and check before sharing.
watch.summary.back: This video comes from a series made with a team of teenage fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. Pictures made by AI can have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In videos made by AI, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check whether the lip movement fits the words. For voices made by AI, listen to the tone of voice and the sounds in the background. The video also shows tools that can help, such as a search that finds where else a picture appears on the internet. But these tools are not always right. A human still needs to think and check before sharing.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and cloned voices in scams (for example a call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). The lesson keeps its examples silly on purpose. Don't show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says a fake was made of them or someone they know, don't discuss the details in class; follow the partner's own safeguarding process.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and copied voices in scams (for example a phone call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). This lesson uses silly examples on purpose. Don't show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says fake content was made about them or someone they know, don't discuss the details in class; follow the partner organisation's child protection procedure.

educatorNotes.0.source: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether the maker says how it was made, whether other trusted sources show the same thing (and didn't all copy one post), and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual glitches (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, never proof: newer tools make fewer of them, and real photos can show odd details too. The study in section 2 is Kamali and others (CHI '25, Northwestern University): more than 50,000 online participants judged 450 AI-made and 149 real images; they called real photographs real in 74% of observations and AI-made images AI-made in 76%, so about one in four was misjudged each way. It is one online study with the authors' own image set, not a general rate. Accept “can't tell yet” as a strong answer. On paper, read the four Greenhill posts aloud and discuss what each source tells you; there is no sorting task.
educatorNotes.0.back: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether its maker says how the content was made, whether other trusted sources show the same thing (and did not all copy one post), and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual oddities (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, not proof: newer tools make them less often, and real photos can also show strange details. The study in section 2 is Kamali and colleagues (CHI '25, Northwestern University): more than 50,000 online participants judged 450 AI-made images and 149 real images; they called real photos real in 74% of observations and AI-made images AI-made in 76%, so about one in four was misjudged in each direction. It is one online study with the authors' own image set, not a general rate. Accept “can't be sure yet” as a strong answer. On paper, read the four Greenhill posts aloud and discuss what each source says; there is no sorting task.

educatorNotes.1.source: Labelled AI work (art, film effects, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as a fake that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Labels can be lost when a picture is reposted (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a labelled post can become misleading when shared without it. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one checked example; learners don't need to go online.
educatorNotes.1.back: AI work with a caption (art, film effects, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as fake content that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Captions can be lost when a picture is reposted (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a post with a caption can mislead when shared without that caption. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one checked example; learners don't need to go online.
